findings.title: Every success criterion maps to a task; sequencing and commit points are sound
findings.description:
Cross-referenced all seven success criteria in `264-slice.context-forge-mcp-tool-bridge.md`:
SC1 (registration + load-time pipeline validity) → Tasks 6, 7.1, 7.4; SC2 (mapped MCP call/args, result
mapping) → Tasks 7.2–7.3; SC3 (real stdio round-trip, `isError`, timeout + WARNING) → Tasks 3, 5.1–5.2,
5.4; SC4 (spawn failure never raises) → Task 5.3; SC5 (live contract test) → Task 8; SC6 (live status
smoke, non-SDK model demo) → Tasks 9.1/9.3, with walkthrough step 4 correctly left open exactly as the
design states; SC7 (full suite, pyright, ruff) → Task 9.2 plus each task's scoped command. No task is
untraceable scope creep — Task 2 and Task 3 are test infrastructure the design's "Tests:" scope names.
Sequencing is acyclic and dependency-correct (config leaf → fixture → bridge → bridge tests → descriptors
→ descriptor tests → live contract → close-out), and tests immediately follow their implementation
(Task 5 after 4, Task 7 after 6). Commit instructions sit at tested, working points, one per task, not
after every step and not only at close-out; they are carried inside the success-criteria checkboxes rather
than as plain `**Commit**:` lines, which matches this project's mandated checklist format (same shape as
263) and is acceptable. No NFR is restated in the parent slice/arch, so absence of a `tests/load/` task and
CI gating for one is correct.

findings.title: Registering the five CF tools breaks an existing test the plan never updates
findings.description:
`tests/tools/test_package.py:11` asserts `set(tools.list_tools()) == {"read_file", "write_file", "bash"}`
and line 22 asserts `len(executors) == 3` after materializing every registered tool. Task 6.4 adds the
side-effect import that registers five more tools at package import, so the full suite goes red at Task 6's
commit — yet no task in the file mentions `tests/tools/test_package.py` (grep for the filename across the
task file returns nothing). This contradicts two of the file's own invariants: "Each task leaves the suite
green" (Sequencing note) and Task 1's "Existing config tests still green" framing for the whole run. Task 6's
success criteria even restate the expected set as "the five `cf_*` names plus the three builtins" without
noting the file that encodes the old expectation. Add an explicit step to Task 6 (or 7.1) to widen
`test_exactly_the_three_builtin_tools_are_registered` / `test_materialize_binds_every_registered_tool` to
the eight-name registry — ideally deriving the expected builtin set from the registry as the file's own
"never hard-coded" principle asks, rather than writing a new magic literal.

findings.title: Two tasks both claim ownership of the spawned process environment
findings.description:
Task 4.1 states the bridge should "use the SDK's `get_default_environment()` as the spawned process env"
while also saying "callers construct `StdioServerParameters`; the bridge does not read config"; Task 6.3
then has the executor build `StdioServerParameters(command, args, cwd=..., env=get_default_environment())`.
Both layers cannot own `env`: if the bridge sets it, it silently overrides whatever a caller put in the
`server: StdioServerParameters` it was handed — which matters because `mcp_bridge.py` is explicitly the
reusable seam for future MCP servers (design D1/Value), where a caller may legitimately need a custom env.
If instead the bridge passes `server` through untouched, Task 4.1's instruction is dead text. Pick one
owner (the caller, consistent with the design's data-flow diagram and Task 6.3) and delete the other
sentence, or state explicitly that the bridge only supplies the default when `server.env is None`.

findings.title: Result-mapping branches are implemented with no test that asserts them
findings.description:
Task 4.2 requires two behaviors beyond the happy path: joining **all** text blocks with `\n`, and noting
non-text blocks by type rather than dropping them. Task 5's fake server only exposes `echo` (single
`TextContent`), `fail`, `sleep`, and `empty`; no tool emits multiple text blocks or a non-text block, and
Task 7 mocks `call_mcp_tool`, so it never exercises `CallToolResult` mapping. Result: a regression that
silently drops image/resource blocks — the exact silent-no-op class the design calls out as the slice-909
lesson — passes the whole suite. Slice success criterion 2 says results are "mapped per the Result mapping
rules", so name the requirement in a test: either add one fixture tool returning two text blocks plus one
non-text block, or unit-test the mapping helper directly against hand-built `CallToolResult` values.

findings.title: Design decision D4 is not pinned by any test
findings.description:
Task 7.1's `test_all_five_registered` runs in whatever environment the developer has, so a registration path
that probed launchability (`shutil.which("npx")`) would still pass on any machine with node — the thing D4
exists to prevent ("a pipeline's validity cannot depend on what's installed on this machine"). One cheap
assertion — set `cf.mcp_command` to an unlaunchable command and assert the five names are still registered —
would pin it. Non-blocking, but it is the cheapest available defense of the decision.

findings.title: Fixture justification names a consumer that does not use it
findings.description:
"Test infrastructure first: tasks 5, 6 both need a real stdio peer" — only Task 5 needs `fake_mcp_server.py`;
Task 6 is descriptor implementation and its tests (Task 7) explicitly run "with no network and no node", while
Task 8 uses the real CF server. A junior implementer following that note could wire `test_cf_tools.py` to the
fake server and break Task 7's stated isolation. Correct the note to "Task 5's tests need a real stdio peer".
